summary.text: Mosses are small, flowerless plants in the division Bryophyta that are non-vascular and typically form dense green clumps or mats.
They reproduce with spores rather than seeds, and the haploid gametophyte is the dominant phase of their life cycle.
Threadlike rhizoids anchor them, and their simple leaves are usually just one cell thick.

facts.label: Main commercial use
facts.value: The main constituent of peat, mostly Sphagnum

items.prompt: A shop sells 'Iceland moss' gathered from a mountain, and a botanist says the name misleads. What does she say it really is?

options.label: A giant moss that grows to 60 centimetres
A liverwort, the closest relative of true mosses
A lichen, which is a symbiotic colony and not related to mosses
A fern whose leaves stay tightly curled

items.explain: Lichens may resemble mosses and share common names, but they are symbiotic colonies and not related to mosses.

items.prompt: A gardener peels a green mat off a stone and finds fine threads holding it on. What are the threads most like?

options.label: Root hairs rather than the thick roots of seed plants
Taproots that reach deep into the stone
Seeds waiting for rain to sprout
Spore stalks, each topped with a capsule

items.explain: Mosses anchor with threadlike rhizoids, comparable to root hairs rather than the more substantial roots of seed plants.

items.prompt: The soft green carpet on a shaded log is mostly which phase of the moss life cycle?

options.label: The diploid sporophyte, as in seed plants
Equal parts gametophyte and sporophyte
The sporophyte capsules on their stalks
The haploid gametophyte, which has a single set of chromosomes

items.explain: In mosses the haploid gametophyte is the dominant phase. Only the sporophyte stage has paired chromosomes, and it is short-lived.

items.prompt: A gardener wants more moss and collects what drops from the plants at the end of the season. What will she actually gather?

options.label: Seeds from tiny flowers
Spores from capsules on unbranched stalks
Pollen-covered fruits
Bulbs from the base of the stem

items.explain: Mosses reproduce with spores, not seeds, and have no flowers. The spores sit in single capsules on unbranched stalks.

items.prompt: A garden-supply firm wants to sell the moss product with the biggest commercial role. What should it stock?

options.label: Edible flour ground from the dried plants
Thread spun into cotton-like fabric
Peat, made mostly from the genus Sphagnum
Cooking oil pressed from the capsules

items.explain: The main commercial significance of mosses is as the main constituent of peat, mostly Sphagnum.

items.prompt: Under a lens a botanist sees a small plant with a clear stem, simple leaves and rhizoids made of many cells. Which group, rather than its look-alike the liverwort, does this point to?

options.label: A moss
A hornwort
A lichen
A liverwort

items.explain: Mosses have multi-cellular rhizoids, unlike liverworts, and a clearly differentiated stem with simple non-vascular leaves points to a moss.

paragraphs.heading: Small green mats
paragraphs.text: Mosses are small plants without flowers that belong to the division Bryophyta. They usually grow as thick green clumps or mats, often where it is damp or shady. Most stand 0.2 to 10 centimetres tall, and there are about 12,000 species. A single moss plant has a stem, branched or unbranched, carrying simple leaves that are mostly just one cell thick.

paragraphs.heading: Without real plumbing
paragraphs.text: Mosses are usually called non-vascular, and unlike vascular plants they lack water-carrying xylem tracheids or vessels. Some species do have conducting tissue, but it is generally poorly developed and built differently, though many mosses have advanced vascular systems. Mosses take in water and nutrients mainly through their leaves. Thread-like rhizoids hold them to the surface they grow on; these resemble root hairs more than true roots, and they can absorb water too.

paragraphs.heading: A life led by the gametophyte
paragraphs.text: Mosses have no flowers or seeds and reproduce with spores. Their life cycle begins when a spore sprouts into a protonema, which is either a mass of fine threads or a flat sheet. The moss plants with stems are gametophytes, and in mosses the gametophyte is the main stage of life. That is the reverse of seed plants and pteridophytes, where the sporophyte stage dominates. After fertilisation a moss grows a sporophyte, an unbranched stalk topped by one capsule of spores, which can photosynthesise but is short-lived and relies on the gametophyte for water and food.

paragraphs.heading: One set of chromosomes
paragraphs.text: Vascular plants are diploid: their body cells hold two sets of chromosomes, each chromosome paired with a partner carrying the same or similar genetic information. Mosses and other bryophytes are haploid instead, with only one copy of each chromosome in a cell. They have paired chromosomes only during the sporophyte stage.

paragraphs.heading: Easy to mistake
paragraphs.text: People often confuse mosses with liverworts, hornworts and lichens. Lichens can look like mosses and even have names like Iceland moss and reindeer moss, yet they are symbiotic colonies unrelated to mosses. Mosses can be told apart from liverworts by their rhizoids, which are made of many cells. In most mosses the spore capsule swells and ripens after its stalk grows longer, while in liverworts this happens before the stalk lengthens.

paragraphs.heading: Why mosses matter
paragraphs.text: Commercially, mosses count most as the main ingredient of peat, mostly from the genus Sphagnum, and they also decorate gardens and florists' displays. In the past people used them as insulation and to soak up liquids, which they can do up to 20 times their own weight. Each year mosses absorb 6.4 billion tons of carbon. They also help stop soil erosion, filter polluted air, cool cities and aid the restoration of habitats and forests.
